judge_analysis:
[votes a3: 3] A. Maintainer test names and whether each patch can be exercised

- `test_clash_parent_link` (`ComplexClashTests`) most likely constructs models with a parent-link OneToOneField and conflicting relation names, then runs Django’s model checks and asserts the appropriate clash is reported (or that a parent link is treated specially in clash detection). It reaches the changed code through `ModelBase` while the model class is created. All three candidates are internal changes to that path; none changes a public signature or rejects a keyword the test would pass. Each can be exercised by this test.
- `test_onetoone_with_parent_model` (`OtherModelTests`) most likely constructs a child model with a OneToOneField targeting its concrete parent, and checks how that field is distinguished from the MTI parent link—potentially including the missing-`parent_link` diagnostic and/or generated parent pointer. This also reaches `ModelBase` directly, and all three candidates accept the same model declarations.

B. Reported broken scenarios

The issue and comments describe: (1) an explicitly marked `document_ptr` declared before another OneToOneField to `Document` is overwritten, causing the latter to be diagnosed as missing `parent_link=True`; (2) reversing the declaration order works, so behavior depends on order; (3) adding `primary_key=True` removes the warning but the model still fails to populate the parent pointer when the field order is unfavorable; and (4) the simpler case of a child with only an unrelated, unmarked OneToOneField to its parent also incorrectly raises the missing-parent-link error.

Candidates 1 and 2 are identical. They fix the first two cases by making an explicitly marked field take precedence, regardless of order. They do not fix case (4): with only the unmarked non-primary-key OneToOneField, it remains the candidate and still triggers the error. They also do not implement the comment’s primary-key-as-parent-link behavior. Candidate 3 prioritizes explicit parent links, treats a primary-key OneToOneField as a fallback, and excludes unrelated unmarked non-primary-key OneToOneFields from the parent-link map. With the latter, Django can generate the separate MTI parent pointer. It therefore covers all reported scenarios.

C. Newly failing repo tests

Candidates 1 and 2 report no newly failing tests. That is not evidence they fix the simpler reported case; retaining the old `test_missing_parent_link` behavior is exactly why they miss it.

Candidate 3 newly fails `test_missing_parent_link`, which expects an unmarked OneToOneField to a parent to raise `ImproperlyConfigured`. That expectation overlaps the reported simpler case: the issue says an unrelated unmarked OneToOneField to the parent must not be mistaken for the parent link. Under the requested change, the old test’s expectation should be revised to check that the unrelated field remains distinct and the MTI link is generated. Per the instruction, this is not a negative against candidate 3. No other newly failing test is reported.

D. Merge judgment

The root problem is not just iteration order: the parent-link discovery code treats every OneToOneField targeting the parent as a parent-link candidate. Candidates 1 and 2 correct which candidate wins only when an explicit marker is also present; they leave the simpler reported failure intact. Candidate 3 uses the explicit `parent_link` marker as the primary signal, preserves a primary-key fallback for migration-state compatibility, and allows an unrelated non-primary-key OneToOneField to coexist with the generated parent pointer. That is the more complete fix for the issue and its comments. It changes the old diagnostic only for the behavior reported as broken and leaves unrelated clash checks and output formats alone.

Candidates 1 and 2 have identical diffs and are indistinguishable from each other; neither is as complete as candidate 3.

- `test_autoclass_content_and_docstring_signature_both` sets `autoclass_content='both'` and similarly invokes `ClassDocumenter`, now with class and constructor docstrings both contributing. It asserts the exact directive and body output, including a constructor signature that remains body text in the existing expected output.

Neither test directly calls `_find_signature` or passes candidate-specific keywords. All three candidates can be exercised through these tests’ normal autodoc calls; candidate 3’s added `all_signatures` parameter is internal and does not make it incompatible.

B. Reported scenarios

The issue reports that overloaded methods in SWIG-wrapped C++ APIs can put multiple signatures at the beginning of a Python docstring, while autodoc extracts only the first. The follow-up describes a Qt API method, `getFeatures`, with four overloads and four associated docstrings, whose generated documentation currently shows the signatures/docstrings appended rather than presenting all overload signatures as signatures. The requested behavior is to recognize all consecutive leading overload signatures and leave the following description as documentation text. The comments do not establish a separate concrete workaround or additional broken input case.

Candidates 2 and 3 collect consecutive signatures for the same name in the matching leading docstring, so both address the reported overload case. Candidate 1 also collects signatures, but additionally combines matches from separate docstrings and allows different valid names; that goes beyond the reported overload scenario and changes class/init behavior.

C. Newly failing tests

Candidate 1 newly fails `test_autoclass_content_and_docstring_signature_both`. That test’s expectation that the constructor signature remains in the body is not behavior the issue reports as broken: the issue asks for multiple overload signatures at the start of one docstring to be extracted, not for signatures from separate class and constructor docstrings to be merged. This is therefore a strong regression. Candidates 2 and 3 report no newly failing repo tests.

D. Behavioral comparison

All candidates keep the existing config gate and format emitted signatures through the normal signature formatter. Candidate 2 most directly fixes the root cause: it recognizes consecutive signatures only when their name matches the first signature, strips those lines from that docstring, and otherwise retains the old behavior of selecting the first matching docstring. That matches the semantics of an overload set and avoids treating a different valid class/constructor name as another overload. Its formatter restores the first signature as the documenter’s arguments afterward.

Candidate 3 also fixes the main method case, and its `all_signatures=False` path preserves the old one-line stripping behavior for `DocstringStripSignatureMixin`. However, its scan permits any name in the broader valid-name list after the first line, so it can consume a different-name signature as part of the same set. Candidate 2’s same-name constraint better preserves unrelated output while still handling the reported inputs. Candidate 1’s cross-docstring aggregation is inconsistent with the test’s existing class/init behavior and is contradicted by its newly failing test.

Candidate 2 best matches the requested behavior, passes both named maintainer tests, and avoids candidate 1’s unrelated output change and candidate 3’s looser name matching.
